title: The Storm Sales Mindset
summary: Walk into every storm door with the inspector frame — disarmed, curious, useful — and your close rate doubles by accident.
body_markdown:
## You are not selling roofs

Let me say this once at the top so it sticks: you are not selling roofs. You are giving people information. Some of them have a $25,000 problem they didn't know about. Some of them don't. Your only job at the door is to find out which one they are, and then help them either way.

Reps who internalize that close more than reps who try to win the door. Every single time. The harder you push, the lower your close rate goes. That's not a motivational saying. That's math we've watched across hundreds of reps.

## The 14-day window

Storms are not a strategy. Storms are a window. The window is 14 days. After day 14, three things happen at once and they're all bad:

1. **Claim filing rates collapse.** Homeowners forget. The damage is out of sight, out of mind.
2. **Your competitors saturate the block.** Reps from 8 other companies have knocked.
3. **Homeowners get exhausted.** They stop opening doors.

If your operation can't mobilize in 72 hours, you're leaving 70% of the available revenue on the table. The reps who get rich in storm sales are the ones who treat hour 6 after the storm differently than hour 60.

## Inspector, not closer

Here is the entire frame in three words: **inspector, not closer.**

A closer walks up to the door with a contract energy. They're already trying to win. The homeowner feels it in three seconds. Door closes.

An inspector walks up to the door with curiosity. They're trying to figure something out. They have a clipboard. They look up at the roof. They ask questions and listen. They take photos. They show the photos. They say "here's what I found."

The close happens later, almost by accident, at the kitchen table after the inspection. Not at the door.

> "Hey, I'm Tyler with Roof Pitcher. I'm not here to sell you anything — I'm doing free 60-second damage checks on this street after the storm Tuesday."

That opener works because every word is true. You really aren't trying to sell anything at this moment. You're trying to inspect. The sentence is the frame.

## Systems beat heroes

Most roofing companies are built around a hero. The owner who can close anyone. The legendary top rep. The sales manager who used to do $4M alone.

Heroes don't scale. Systems do.

A 23-year-old rep with the right script and the right neighborhood will outclose your hero in three months, because the system doesn't have bad days, doesn't drink the night before, doesn't take rejection home. The hero gets injured, gets bored, gets poached, or just gets tired. The system keeps running.

The entire Storm Sales Mastery course is teaching you a system. Run it in order. Don't skip steps because you think you're a hero. Heroes lose to systems. We have receipts.

## The ethical floor

Storm sales is the part of roofing that gets a bad rap. You know why. There are reps out there using fake urgency, scaring homeowners about leaks that don't exist, telling people the adjuster "missed something" when they didn't.

That behavior wins one job and loses three. Roofing is a referral business. Burn one block, you've burned the next three.

The ethical floor is simple:

- If you walk away from a door feeling slimy, you did it wrong.
- If you walk away feeling like an inspector, you did it right — whether or not you got the appointment.
- Never lie about damage you didn't find.
- Never invent urgency that doesn't exist.
- Never bad-mouth the previous contractor or the adjuster.

This isn't a values lecture. It's a profit-and-loss statement. Reps who stay above the line build 5-year careers in this industry. Reps who don't are gone in 14 months and burning the territory they leave behind.

## The homeowner is exhausted

Last thing: the homeowner is not your enemy. They have had three guys knock today. They are tired. They are skeptical. They are not bad people for being short with you.

Your job at the door is to make their afternoon easier, not harder. Disarm them. Give them 60 seconds of useful information. Either book the inspection or leave gracefully and move on. Don't take it personally. Don't argue. Don't push.

The ones who don't book today often book in week 2 when they realize you were the only one who didn't pressure them. Patience is a storm sales superpower nobody talks about.

## What this means for tomorrow

Go into the field with two intentions:

1. **Make every door a useful experience for the homeowner, regardless of outcome.**
2. **Trust the system. Run the 7-Question Knock. Don't freelance.**

Do those two things and the math takes over. You'll close at industry-leading rates and you'll sleep well at night, which most storm reps can't say.

Welcome to the system. Let's go to work.
key_takeaways: You sell the inspection at the door — never the roof.
Storm sales is a 14-day window. Move in 72 hours.
Inspector frame, not closer frame. Curiosity wins.
Systems beat heroes. Run the playbook, don't freelance.
If you feel slimy walking away, you did it wrong.

quiz.q: What is the actual product you are selling at the door?
quiz.explanation: If you leave a door with a booked inspection, you won. The roof sale happens later at the kitchen table.

choices: Insurance requires claims to be filed within 14 days
Hail damage becomes invisible after 14 days
Claim filing rates collapse and competitors saturate after 14 days
Adjusters refuse to assess older damage
quiz.explanation: Filing rates collapse, competitors saturate, and homeowners get exhausted. The window is operational, not regulatory.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT part of the inspector frame?
choices: Carrying a clipboard and taking notes
Looking up at the roof before knocking
Telling the homeowner you can save them thousands
Asking questions and listening more than talking
quiz.explanation: "Save you thousands" is closer language. Inspectors find things; they don't sell outcomes at the door.

quiz.q: What's the cost of pushing too hard at the door?
choices: Lower close rate plus reputation damage that burns referral territory
quiz.explanation: Roofing is a referral business. Burning one block burns the next three. Push-style reps lose 3 jobs for every 1 they win.

homework: Tomorrow, knock 20 doors with one rule: do not mention 'roof replacement' once. Only inspect, inform, and offer next steps. Track how many bookings you get vs your last 20.
